etymologies.etymologyHTML: Probably North Germanic origin. This etymology is incomplete. You can help Wiktionary by elaborating on the origins of this term.

quote.citation: 1592, William Shakespeare, King Richard III:
quote.text: Some tardy cripple bore the countermand, / That came too lag to see him buried.

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: the lag end of my life

definitions.definition: Last made; hence, made of refuse; inferior.

quote.citation: 1690, John Dryden, Don Sebastian, King of Portugal:
quote.text: We know your thoughts of us, that laymen are lag souls, and rubbish of remaining clay.

definitions.definition: (countable) A gap, a delay; an interval created by something not keeping up; a latency.

quote.citation: 1995, Donald R. DeGlopper, “Introduction”, in Lukang: Commerce and Community in a Chinese City‎[1], State University of New York Press, →ISBN, →LCCN, →OCLC, page 5:
quote.text: Although this work is now presented to the world at large, people who read through it before publication severally raised some issues that should be addressed. These resolve around the lag between the field research and the publication of the monograph, a period of rather more than two decades; the use or non-use of various academic forms of terminology, frames of reference, modes of analysis, or "theoretical paradigms"; and my use of the present tense to describe a place that is most certainly not that way now.

quote.citation: 2004 May 10, The New Yorker Online,:
quote.text: During the Second World War, for instance, the Washington Senators had a starting rotation that included four knuckleball pitchers. But, still, I think that some of that was just a generational lag.

quote.citation: 1999, Loyd Case, Building the ultimate game PC:
quote.text: Whatever the symptom, lag is a drag. But what causes it? One cause is delays in getting the data from your PC to the game server.

quote.citation: 2001, Patricia M. Wallace, The psychology of the Internet:
quote.text: When the lag is low, 2 or 3 seconds perhaps, Internet chatters seem reasonably content.

quote.citation: 2002, Marty Cortinas, Clifford Colby, The Macintosh bible:
quote.text: Latency, or lag, is an unavoidable part of Internet gaming.

definitions.definition: (UK, Ireland, slang, archaic) One sentenced to transportation for a crime.
(UK, Ireland, slang) A prisoner, a criminal.

quote.citation: 1934, P. G. Wodehouse, Thank You, Jeeves:
quote.text: On both these occasions I had ended up behind the bars, and you might suppose that an old lag like myself would have been getting used to it by now.

quote.citation: 1986, John le Carré, A Perfect Spy:
quote.text: He sat with his great head tipped forward, scowling with a lag's sullenness, and I swear he had closed off his hearing with his thinking and hadn't heard us coming. 'Father,' said Pym.

quote.citation: 2017, Anna Leask, Behind Bars: Real-life stories from inside New Zealand's prisons:
quote.text: I wasn't scared any more; the second lag wasn't easy, but I wasn't really scared of anything.  […]  So in my later lags, when I walked into prison everyone had heard about me.

definitions.definition: (snooker) A method of deciding which player is to start. Both players simultaneously strike a cue ball from the baulk line to hit the top cushion and rebound down the table; the player whose ball finishes closest to the baulk cushion wins.
One who lags; that which comes in last.

quote.citation: 1725, Homer, “Book IX”, in [William Broome], transl., The Odyssey of Homer. […], volume II, London:  […]  Bernard Lintot, →OCLC, page 226, line 526:
quote.text: the lag of all the flock

definitions.definition: The fag-end; the rump; hence, the lowest class.

quote.citation: c. 1605–1608, William Shakespeare, “The Life of Tymon of Athens”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene vi], page 89, column 2:
quote.text: The reſt of your Fees, O Gods, the Senators of Athens, together with the common lagge of People, what is amiſſe in them, you Gods, make ſuteable for deſtruction.

definitions.definition: A stave of a cask, drum, etc.; especially (engineering) one of the narrow boards or staves forming the covering of a cylindrical object, such as a boiler, or the cylinder of a carding machine or steam engine.
To fail to keep up (the pace), to fall behind.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “(please specify the book), Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: Behind her farre away a Dwarfe did lag, / That lasie seemd in being ever last, / Or wearied with bearing of her bag / Of needments at his backe.

quote.citation: 1616, George Chapman, The Odysseys of Homer:
quote.text: Lazy beast! / Why last art thou now? Thou hast never used / To lag thus hindmost

quote.citation: 1717, The Metamorphoses of Ovid translated into English verse under the direction of Sir Samuel Garth by John Dryden, Alexander Pope, Joseph Addison, William Congreve and other eminent hands
quote.text: While he, whose tardy feet had lagg'd behind, / Was doom'd the sad reward of death to find.

quote.citation: 1798, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, The Rime of the Ancient Mariner in seven parts:
quote.text: Brown skeletons of leaves that lag / My forest-brook along

quote.citation: 2004 April 5, The New Yorker,:
quote.text: Over the next fifty years, by most indicators dear to economists, the country remained the richest in the world. But by another set of numbers—longevity and income inequality—it began to lag behind Northern Europe and Japan.

definitions.definition: To cover (for example, pipes) with felt strips or similar material (referring to a time lag effect in thermal transfer).

quote.citation: 1941 April, “British Locomotive Developments”, in Railway Magazine, page 173:
quote.text: Spun glass mattresses are used for lagging the boiler, which has three Ross pop safety valves on the front ring.

quote.citation: c. 1974, Philip Larkin, The Building:
quote.text: Outside seems old enough: / Red brick, lagged pipes, and someone walking by it / Out to the car park, free.

definitions.definition: (computing, informal, video games) To respond slowly.
(UK, slang, archaic) To transport as a punishment for crime.

quote.citation: 1847, Thomas De Quincey, Secret Societies":
quote.text: She lags us if we poach.

definitions.definition: (UK, slang, archaic) To arrest or apprehend.

quote.citation: 1925 July – 1926 May, A[rthur] Conan Doyle, “(please specify the chapter number)”, in The Land of Mist (eBook no. 0601351h.html), Australia: Project Gutenberg Australia, published April 2019:
quote.text: "We must get the old dear out," said Lord Roxton to Malone. "He'll be had for manslaughter if we don't. What I mean, he's not responsible - he'll sock someone and be lagged for it."

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause to lag; to slacken.

quote.citation: 1632, Thomas Heywood, The Iron Age:
quote.text: The weight would lagge thee that art wont to flye.
